## Two points from the literature {#two-sentences-worth-keeping}

::: {.claimcard}
"the common single-path analyses in social and behavioural research should not be simply assumed to be robust to alternative analyses" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]
:::

::: {.claimcard}
A blueprint: precise question → causal reasoning (DAG) → multiverse → sensitivity analysis [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial]
:::

::: {.small}
- Same-conclusion robustness and same-*number* robustness are different bars
- Justifiability is the criterion – choose with reasons, show the spread
:::

::: notes
The first point comes from the Multi100 paper: single-path analyses should not simply be assumed robust. And notice what preregistration did and did not do for you today. It protected your choice from being opportunistic, but it gave your preregistered dot no special status inside the curve. The preregistration made your one path defensible, and the curve showed that it was still one path among eight hundred and sixty-four, so a report needs the preregistered path and the space around it together. From Auspurg and Brüderl comes the constructive recipe we followed – precise question, explicit assumptions, multiverse, sensitivity. And keep the two robustness standards apart in your own writing: same *conclusion*, which was seventy-four per cent in Multi100, and same *number*, which was thirty-four. When you claim robustness, say which one you mean.
:::

- **Yours now.** A rendered report with its preregistration block. An estimand statement and a causal graph that you wrote yourself. Two dots on the class chart, one exploratory from Task 4 and one preregistered from Task 5.
- **Read.** The three *Nature* papers of 2026 [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial], the glossary [@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms], @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial, @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand, @LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne and @Teney2016DoesEUEconomic.
- **Explore.** The companion modules of the case, among them panel data, multilevel models, Bayesian estimation, causal graphs, the multiverse debate, and repositories and preregistration. R, the IDE, Quarto, and Git and GitHub on the AR4DS site. The Multi100 data. The documentation of `fixest` and `ggdag`.
- **Keep going locally.** The research-software and open-research teams at your university, and a ReproducibiliTea journal club near you.
- Everything is on the course site, and everything is open – fork any of it

You take home a rendered report with a preregistration block in it, an estimand statement and a causal graph that you wrote for a real published claim, and two dots on the class chart, one exploratory from Task 4 and one preregistered from Task 5. The website on screen has everything else – the readings, the data, the companion modules, the specification-curve reading, and the full SCORE dossier on the paper if you want to dig further. Two pointers for keeping the habit alive wherever you work: most universities have a research-software engineering team and an open-research or library data service that run training like today's, and ReproducibiliTea journal clubs meet in dozens of cities – if there is not one near you, they will help you start one.
